title: Belt stood still for 107s with freight on it
what: From 8:51 to 10:37 the freight on the belt did not move, with 5 people in view (6 minutes of crew time spent waiting). Across the clip the belt stood still 5 times, 4 min 58 s in total (17% of the time).
so_what: A stopped belt idles everyone on the line at once, at both ends. It is the most expensive kind of wait, and it does not show up as anyone doing anything wrong.
recommendation: Find out who stops the belt and why: an awkward item, a full cart, or the feeding end pausing. If stops cluster around oversized items, a set-down area off the belt would let it keep running.

title: About 2 people working whether 5 or 7 were present
what: Average number handling freight at each crew size (belt stops excluded): 3 present: 1.0, 4 present: 1.6, 5 present: 2.0, 6 present: 2.0, 7 present: 2.0.
so_what: Extra people did not find work to do. That points to a pace set by something fixed, such as the number of scan points or the rate freight arrives, rather than headcount.
recommendation: Add a scan or pick-off point so more people can work in parallel; that is the larger lever. Running with 5 frees little by comparison. Crew size and workload are confounded in one clip, so treat this as a test to run.

title: Crew size ran opposite to the workload
what: In the 2 minutes from 4:00 about 6.4 people were in view and the belt was 9% covered. In the 2 minutes from 26:00 there were 3.5 and it was 38% covered. Across the clip, the more people were present, the emptier the belt tended to be.
so_what: People were at this line when the freight was not, and fewer were there when it arrived. The same headcount, timed to the freight, would mean less waiting early and less backlog later.
recommendation: Find out where people went and what triggered it. If staffing follows a fixed routine rather than the belt, trial a simple rule: join this line when the belt is more than a third covered, leave when it runs empty.

title: Belt ran empty for 51s with 6 waiting at it
what: Between 1:23 and 2:13 almost nothing was on the belt while 6 people stood at it (3 minutes of crew time spent waiting).
so_what: The crew in view was not the bottleneck here: the unloading end feeding the belt was. Adding people at this end would not have moved more freight.
recommendation: Look at the unloading end feeding the belt for this period (it is outside this camera's view). If it is short-handed, moving one person there from this crew is the cheapest fix.

title: 6 workers present, 1 handling freight for 101s
what: From 5:57 to 7:37, 6 people were in view but only 1 appeared to be handling freight. Together they waited for 6 minutes of crew time.
so_what: This is paid labour with nothing in front of it. If the pattern repeats across a shift, this crew is larger than the work reaching it.
recommendation: The belt was 37% covered at the time, so freight was available. Check what held them up: full cages, no space to put freight down, or unclear who takes what. If it repeats, move one person to where the constraint is.

recommendation: Use this as the benchmark. Compare crew size and how freight arrived here with the periods of waiting.
